wordings: As 36 CFR 294.12 and 13 already include provisions for road development and tree removal to support wildfire protection and other conditions deemed necessary and aligned with the statute per the responsible forest official, the stated intent of this proposal to alleviate local agencies to make decisions seems disingenuous.

By definition, they lack the roads that are strongly associated with human-caused fire ignitions, while the Rule’s existing exceptions provide mechanisms for addressing legitimate wildfire and public-safety needs.
Concerns about fire risk and essential utility projects have already been addressed in the existing regulations under 36 CFR § 294.12 and § 294.13.

Existing authorities within the Roadless Rule under 36 CFR 294 12(b) and 13(b) with environmental review, allow for the necessary exceptions for protection of public health and safety from natural disasters such as wildfire and floods as well as for wildlife/T&E species habitat restoration/maintenance.
Explain why existing Roadless Rule exceptions cannot address legitimate wildfire and public-safety needs.

Explain why the existing provisions in 36 CFR 294.12 and 294.13 do not allow those projects, including whether small-diameter thinning, prescribed fire, fire-line construction, or the imminent-threat exception was considered.
Flawed Premise Regarding Wildfire Mitigation and Road Infrastructure(Addressing 36 CFR § 294.12):

Generally, road construction and industrial timber harvest are not allowed, but both the National Roadless Rule and the Idaho Roadless Rule allow for hazardous fuel reduction projects around communities.

However, the existing 2001 Roadless Rule already contains clear, commonsense provisions that permit road construction and maintenance when necessary—including for public safety, firefighter access, response to natural disasters, and hazardous fuels management near communities.

Initiate a more limited rulemaking that amends 36 CFR 294 Subpart B to give local units clearer, faster tools for hazardous fuels reduction and forest-health treatments where those tools are genuinely needed — without eliminating the core prohibition on road construction and reconstruction in inventoried roadless areas.

It shows that the existing exceptions at §§ 294.12(b)(1) and 294.13(b)(1)(ii) already permit fuels reduction and emergency road access, and that the Ninth Circuit upheld use of the fuels exception on the Los Padres National Forest in 2024.

Kentucky Heartwood adds that the existing Roadless Rule already “allows for necessary forest management and the construction of roads as needed to address fires, floods, or other catastrophic events, and other circumstances like the need to connect communities.”

Reasoning: Emergency exceptions allow local forest managers to respond to urgent wildfire risks on a case-by-case basis without subjecting 44+ million acres of intact public lands to permanent industrial access and capital maintenance liabilities.

The 2001 Roadless Rule already contains narrow, well-defined exceptions under 36 CFR Section 294.13(b)(1) that explicitly allow the Forest Service to harvest timber and conduct hazardous fuels reduction to protect communities, provided it is done without constructing permanent, ecosystem-disrupting road networks.

The 2001 Roadless Rule explicitly contains built-in exceptions allowing active management and targeted tree cutting to reduce the risk of uncharacteristic wildfire or restore ecosystem health (see 36 CFR § 294.13(b)(1)).

The 2001 rule already contains exceptions for road construction needed for wildfire response, public health and safety, and other circumstances (36 CFR 294.12), so the claim that the rule blocks fire management does not hold up against the rule's own text or the agency's own history of approving treatments in roadless areas.

The Roadless Rule contains exceptions for cutting small-diameter timber to reduce the risk of uncharacteristic wildfire (36 CFR 294.13(b)(1)) and for roads needed to protect public health and safety from imminent threats such as fire (36 CFR 294.12(b)(1)).

The existing Roadless Rule already contains exceptions allowing certain activities to address threats to health and safety, catastrophic events, hazardous road conditions, and some ecological management needs.

The existing Roadless Rule already contains exceptions, and responsible management should allow agencies to address legitimate safety or ecological emergencies without abandoning protections across millions of acres.

The existing rule already contains explicit exceptions (36 CFR §§ 294.12–294.13) permitting road construction and timber cutting to protect public safety and reduce hazardous fuels during emergencies.

The proposal itself acknowledges the 2001 Rule already allows exceptions for fire and forest-health work, but says those exceptions were "expected to be infrequent" and hard to use because of review requirements.⁵ That's appears to be a process problem, not something requiring repealing protections on 58.5 million acres.

wordings: Absence of Quantified Nationwide Cumulative Timber Harvest, Road Construction, Sedimentation, and Fragmentation Analysis The Draft EIS states the purpose of the proposed rescission in terms of "changing and localized conditions, such as increasing wildfire risk, the spread of insect and disease infestations, and the need for community protection in the wildland-urban interface" (DEIS Vol. I, p. 18), and asserts that the 2001 Roadless Rule "has contributed to the lack of active management of the national forests" (p. 19).

According to the USDA Forest Service (2026a), the proposed rollback of the Roadless Rule would increase flexibility in management, including where and when to reduce wildfire risk based on local conditions.
According to the draft EIS proposed action, the rule rescission is more responsive to decreasing wildfire risk and the need for community protection in the wildland-urban interface.

As for the wildfire debate, the rationale for reexamining the rule is that local managers need more flexibility to reduce wildfire risk across the 28 million roadless acres it identifies as high or very high fire-risk zones.

As stated in the Draft Environmental Impact Report (DEIS), the Rationale for the Proposed Rule is to reinstate “….important management tools for key areas where there are needs or opportunities to address overgrown and fuel-loaded national forests.”
Flawed Wildfire Rationale: The Draft Environmental Impact Statement (DEIS) asserts that local management flexibility is needed to address wildfire risk.

For example, if fire management is truly a primary aim of the proposed rule rescission, the Forest Service might consider proposing an amendment to the existing rule that allows for strategic maintenance of existing roads or limited roadway expansion that is specifically planned to help control wildfires but limiting public vehicular access whereby literature indicates wildfires are more likely to be generated (e.g., Applet et al. 2026 at https://doi.org/10.1186/s42408-026-00450-2).
I also do not believe that eliminating the Roadless Rule is necessary to responsibly address wildfire risk or legitimate forest-management needs.

I recognize the need to actively manage national forests, reduce wildfire risks, and give local managers sufficient flexibility, but the Forest Service’s own analysis indicates that the additional management opportunities created by rescission would be modest and localized.

I understand the argument that rescinding the national rule could give local land managers greater flexibility to address issues such as wildfire, insects, disease, timber management, and local economic needs.

If additional flexibility is warranted, amend 36 CFR 294.13(b)(1) by adopting the standard already in force at 36 CFR 294.24(b)(1)(iii) — "To reduce the risk of uncharacteristic wildland fire effects to an at-risk community or municipal water supply system" — rather than rescinding the subpart.

One of the major arguments for repealing the Roadless Rule is that USDA USFS local managers need more flexibility to reduce wildfire risk across the 28 million roadless acres it identifies as high or very high fire-risk zones.

Still, the DEIS claims that rescission will allow for fire related management, as if the 2001 Roadless Rule doesn't allow for forest management activities, including timber harvest, to reduce the risk of uncharacteristic wildfire, as well as to restore habitat for sensitive fish and wildlife species. It does.

That approach would still strip protection from roughly half of the nation's roadless national forests, and the rule already gives local land managers the flexibility they need to address genuine wildfire risk.
The DEIS identifies increased flexibility for wildfire management as a potential benefit of rescission, particularly in the wildland-urban interface.

The Draft EIS states the purpose of the proposed rescission in terms of "changing and localized conditions, such as increasing wildfire risk, the spread of insect and disease infestations, and the need for community protection in the wildland-urban interface" (DEIS Vol. I, p. 18), and asserts that the 2001 Roadless Rule "has contributed to the lack of active management of the national forests" (p. 19).

The Federal Register notice for the Proposed Rule states, “There is a need to increase local management flexibility and, where necessary, allow for active management to respond to changing and localized conditions, such as increasing wildfire risk, the spread of insect and disease infestations, and the need for community protection in the wildland-urban interface.”

The Forest Services’ rationale for the proposal is that “prohibitions from the rule have removed important management tools for key areas where there are needs or opportunities to address overgrown and fuel-loaded national forests” as stated in Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation 36 CFR Part 294.

The Purpose and Need for Action in 91 Fed. Reg. 53827 (Aug. 20, 2026), RIN 0596-AD66, Docket FS-2025-000 subpart D).includes management flexibility … to respond to changing and localized conditions such as increasing wildfire risk” (see: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/20/2026-16965/special-areas-roadless-area-conservation) and increase logging and “access for minerals or energy uses” ” (see: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/20/2026-16965/special-areas-roadless-area-conservation) (printed page 53828).

The USDA has cited this as part of its rationale for reexamining the rule, arguing that local managers need more flexibility to reduce wildfire risk across the 28 million roadless acres it identifies as high or very high fire-risk zones.
The USDA is rescinding the roadless rule in order to allow local management flexibility, reduce wildfire risk, and open 4.8 million acres for potential timber harvest.
The proposal assumes that removing national protections will provide greater management flexibility and help address issues such as wildfire risk, forest health concerns, and access needs.

The proposal identifies wildfire risk, drought, insects, and disease as reasons for greater management flexibility, but greater flexibility is not itself evidence that development of roadless areas is the most effective way to address these problems.
The proposal indicates fire mitigation as part of the local flexibly management.

The proposed rule says that one of the main reasons to rescind this rule is in response to changing and localized conditions, such as increasing wildfire risk, the spread of insect and disease infestations, and the need for community protection in the wildland-urban interface.

The purpose and need for action section of the proposed rescission claims that rescinding the Roadless Rule is necessary to afford “increased management flexibility” for forest maintenance and claims roadbuilding is necessary to address “increasing wildfire risk, the spread of insect and disease infestations, and the need for community protection in the wildland-urban interface.”

The stated purpose and need for it is to return “decision-making authority to local leaders [to ensure] that issues such as reducing wildfire risks and forest health are addressed based on local conditions rather than a one-size fits all regulation,” however, this action would threaten forest health and exacerbate wildfire risks by putting pressure on rural, local decision-makers who may feel a responsibility to open up lands to irresponsible developments for short-term profits.

Under the Rationale section of this proposal, it acknowledges maintaining “ecological integrity,” mitigating wildfire risk, and increasing access for forest/insect/disease management purposes, while simultaneously highlighting the need to access timber and mineral resources.

While the proposal acknowledges several pressing issues facing our forests, such as increased wildfire activity, increased pest pressure, and the need for regionally adaptive management, it fails to address one of the most critical underlying factors: climate change.

The proposed rule says that one of the main reasons to rescind this rule is in response to changing and localized conditions, such as increasing wildfire risk, the spread of insect and disease infestations, and the need for community protection in the wildland-urban interface.

The purpose and need for action section of the proposed rescission claims that rescinding the Roadless Rule is necessary to afford “increased management flexibility” for forest maintenance and claims roadbuilding is necessary to address “increasing wildfire risk, the spread of insect and disease infestations, and the need for community protection in the wildland-urban interface.”

The stated purpose and need for it is to return “decision-making authority to local leaders [to ensure] that issues such as reducing wildfire risks and forest health are addressed based on local conditions rather than a one-size fits all regulation,” however, this action would threaten forest health and exacerbate wildfire risks by putting pressure on rural, local decision-makers who may feel a responsibility to open up lands to irresponsible developments for short-term profits.

Under the Rationale section of this proposal, it acknowledges maintaining “ecological integrity,” mitigating wildfire risk, and increasing access for forest/insect/disease management purposes, while simultaneously highlighting the need to access timber and mineral resources.

While the proposal acknowledges several pressing issues facing our forests, such as increased wildfire activity, increased pest pressure, and the need for regionally adaptive management, it fails to address one of the most critical underlying factors: climate change.

wordings: Although proponents of rolling back the Roadless Rule claim it is needed for wildfire management, the peer-reviewed science shows the opposite A separate national analysis (Balch et al., PNAS 2017) found that 84% of all U.S. wildfires are human-caused.

Although there are narratives claiming that removing this rule is beneficial to forest health through “responsible active management”—roadbuilding actually increases wildfire risk, as 90% of wildfires start within 1/2 mile of a road.

Contrary to USDA’s claim that this rescission will reduce wildfire risk, research shows wildfires are four times more likely to start in roaded areas than in unroaded tracts, and nearly 85% of wildfires are human-caused, often igniting near roads.

Contrary to some arguments in favor of rescinding the rule, decades of studies have shown that roadless areas have up to four times fewer wildfire incidents (Aplet, Hartger & Dietz 2026) and that humans are responsible for the overwhelming majority of wildfires (Balch et al. 2017), so it follows that restricting human access to remote wildlands will reduce wildfire incidence.

Contrary to the USDA's claim that this rescission will help the agency reduce fire risk, more roads are likely to mean more fires as 85% of wildfires are human-caused, and most ignite within a few hundred feet of roads.
Despite the rescission being proposed to decrease the likelihood of wildfires, it has been found that 84% of US wildfires are caused by humans, with the main vector being roads (Aplet et al., 2026).

Equally important, the current administration's claims that abolishing the Roadless Rule will supposedly mitigate fires are absolutely false; it's been found between 84 and 88% of all wildfires in the US are caused by humans and ignite close to pre-existing roads.

Fire Risk Management: Justifying the removal of roadless protections on the grounds of fire prevention contradicts the Forest Service’s own findings showing that nearly 90% of wildland fires start near roads.
I strongly oppose the Trump administration’s plans to rescind the Roadless Area Conservation Rule and increase the wildfire risks there by 400 percent (99 percent are human caused).

If anything, the Roadless Rule *reduces* wildfire risk by limiting the extent of motorized access to the landscape; after all, over 90% of fires begin within half a mile of a road, and ignitions are roughly four times more likely near roads than in roadless areas (Forest Service data, 2026 Fire Ecology study).
In reality, this rescinding of protections could actually increase wildfire risk, as nearly 85% of U.S. wildfires are human-caused, and roads would just act as facilitators.
Increased Wildfire Risk: While the administration frames this rollback as a tool for wildfire mitigation, data shows that 90% of wildfires are human-caused.
Increased Wildfire Risk: While the agency cites wildfire risk reduction as a rationale for rescission, studies consistently show that nearly 90% of wildland fires originate near road access points.

Increased Wildfire Risk: While the stated rationale for the rollback includes wildfire management, data shows that wildfires are four times more likely to start near roads, with roughly 90% starting within half a mile of a road.
It would increase wildfire risk rather than reduce it--most California wildfires are human caused.

Moreover, wildfires will likely increase, rather than decrease under your proposed rule as 78% of human-caused wildfires start within a half mile of a road, and your repeal is intended to allow more road construction (temporary and permanent) in roadless areas.

Our research together has shown that most wildfires are caused by humans and most fires start with close proximity to roadways, so the roadless rule is protecting us (https://earthjustice.org/feature/timeline-of-the-roadless-rule, https://defenders.org/roadless-rule, https://www.outdooralliance.org/roadless, https://www.pfpi.net/2026/08/new-analysis-measures-benefits-of-intact-roadless-forests/).
Repealing the roadless rule would also increase wildfire risk as 85% of fires are estimated to be started by humans.
Roads are also where most human-caused fires start (Aplet et al. 2026, https://doi.org/10.1186/s42408-026-00450-2)—rescinding the roadless rule will do more to cause fires than prevent them.
Roads are the primary ignition source for wildfires, with 90% of fires starting near roadways; rescinding the rule would increase fire hazards rather than mitigate them.

Since 90 percent of wildfires are started by people and 78 percent are within one-half mile of a road (according to the Western Fire Chiefs Association), the wildfire risk would likely be increased by rescinding the roadless rule.

The DEIS did not properly justify the need for this rescission based on wildfire management, because as we know two-thirds of human caused wildfires in my home state of California are started near roads and 95% of wildfires are caused by humans.
The USDA's claim that rescission would reduce wildfire risk is inaccurate, as the vast majority of wildfires (85%) are caused by humans--and usually start very close to roads.

The claim made by the current administration that repealing the Roadless Rule aids in wildfire prevention contradicts established scientific research, which demonstrates that 85% of wildfires are human-caused.
They tout the proposed repeal as an effort to mitigate wildfires through an expansion of access, while ignoring the fact that 84% of wildfires are human caused (Balch et al, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci.).
This rule claims to that a goal is to manage areas to address increased wildfire risk, but 80% of wildfires are human caused.

We know that most fires (over 84%) are started by humans within 50 meters of roads; that forest ecosystems maintain their own balance and succession of habitats which human intervention simply destroys; and, that the Rule was originally created precisely because local control did not adequately protect our forests.

We prioritize wildfire for profitable gain and if the roadless rule is rescinded due to the argument of wildfire prevention, then we have failed to understand that 80% of wildfires occur within 800 meters of roads.

Increased soil erosion and compaction due to timber harvests could lead to a 6 to 9 times greater likelihood of landslides and debris flows adjacent to forest roads (page 111).
Landslides and debris flows are 9 times more likely adjacent to forest roads, and rescinding the Roadless Rule would increase the amount of roads in our landscape (USDA Proposed Rule, p.111).
Landslides are a natural hazard in Southeast Alaska which is increased with road construction on overstepped slopes.
Over the years, multiple landslides along Canyon Creek have undercut the road and severely impacted stream quality and the presence of fish in those stretches.
Paving roads through Mogan Ridge will drastically increase sediment levels.

Reporting in Smithsonian magazine (Ben Goldfarb, "The Case for Destroying Old Forest Roads," March 2024) notes that, in 1995, storm-triggered landslides tied to old logging roads in Idaho's Nez Perce-Clearwater National Forest produced more than 900 landslides that buried streams under more than 50,000 dump trucks' worth of sediment — a preview of the kind of long-term damage new road construction risks recreating elsewhere.
Road building and forest cutting increases landslides in mountainous areas which is where many of the roadless areas are (Swanson and Dyrness 1975, Tanyaş et al. 2022).

Road construction clears riparian vegetation, exposing slopes that erode soil resulting in sediment entering streams, jeopardizing water quality throughout numerous potentially impacted areas throughout Pisgah and Nantahala Forests, including the South Mills River area in Pisgah.
Roads, logging, and ground disturbance can increase erosion, sedimentation, landslides, and chemical runoff, particularly in Oregon’s steep terrain.
The DEIS itself notes that landslide effects persist when a road permanently undercuts unstable soils or landforms.
Western North Carolina’s steep gradients, thin erodible soils, and extreme precipitation make road cuts a leading source of sedimentation and slope failure.

Widespread deforestation and road construction from historical surface mining and other activities have already increased flood risk for downstream communities, as demonstrated by the 2022 floods in Eastern Kentucky.

wordings: A 2021 analysis found that lands protected by the roadless rule can provide suitable habitat to half (57%) of wildlife species of conservation concern.

A 2021 study in Global Ecology and Conservation found that 308 of 537 wildlife species of conservation concern in the contiguous United States (57%) had at least some suitable habitat in inventoried roadless areas.

A later national analysis found that 77% of roadless areas had the potential to conserve threatened, endangered, or imperiled species, and that a handful of roadless areas hold a large share of suitable habitat for some species of concern (Dietz et al. 2021.
A recent study found that 308 of 537 species of conservation concern in the United States have habitat contained within our Inventoried Roadless Areas (Dietz et al., 2021).
According to Loucks et al. (2003), “77% of inventoried roadless areas have the potential to conserve threatened, endangered, or imperiled species.”
Adding unprotected roadless areas to protected areas markedly reduces poorly-represented species of conservation concern. — Dietz et al., 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gecco.2021.e01943)”

Additionally, Dietz et al. find that, “Of the 537 wildlife species of conservation concern in the contiguous United States, 308 species (57%) have at least some suitable habitat in one or more inventoried roadless areas.

Conservation Ecology 7(2): 5. [online] URL: http://www.consecol.org/vol7/iss2/art5/) 77% of inventoried roadless areas in the U.S. have the potential to provide critical habitat for threatened, endangered and imperiled species.
Dietz et al. (2021) examined 537 wildlife species of conservation concern and found that 308 species, or 57%, had suitable habitat within Inventoried Roadless Areas.

Dietz et al. (2021) found that over half of species of considerable concern have suitable habitat within inventoried roadless areas, despite these areas covering only 2% of the continental US, with every single inventoried roadless area providing habitat for at least 2 species of special concern.

Dietz et al. (Global Ecology and Conservation, 2023) mapped 1,719 terrestrial species against Forest Service Inventoried Roadless Areas and found that although these areas make up only ~2% of land in the lower 48, they overlap with habitat for 57% of species listed as vulnerable, threatened, or endangered — every single inventoried roadless area studied provided habitat for at least two species of conservation concern.
Dietz et al., Global Ecology and Conservation 32, e01943 (2021), found that 308 of 537 species of conservation concern—57 percent—have suitable habitat within inventoried roadless areas.

Dietz, M. S., Barnett, K., Belote, R. T., & Aplet, G. H. (2021), "The importance of U.S. national forest roadless areas for vulnerable wildlife species," Global Ecology and Conservation vol. 32, doi:10.1016/j.gecco.2021.e01943, examined 537 terrestrial vertebrate wildlife species of conservation concern in the contiguous United States and found that "308 species, or 57%, have at least some suitable habitat in inventoried roadless areas, even though inventoried roadless areas only cover 2% of the area of the contiguous United States."

Fish and wildlife. A study in Global Ecology and Conservation (Dietz et al., 2021) found that inventoried roadless areas cover about 2 percent of the land in the lower 48 states yet provide habitat for 308 of the 537 species, or 57 percent, that are listed as threatened or endangered or are candidates under the Endangered Species Act.

I request supplementation of the analysis under 7 CFR 1b.7(f)(2)(iii): incorporate the Dietz et al. 2021 finding into the habitat discussion of the affected environment, add the study to the DEIS References Cited, and carry a roadless-specific measure of species-of-conservation-concern habitat through the effects analysis for each alternative, including the no-action alternative.

In "The Importance of U.S. National Forest Roadless Areas for Vulnerable Wildlife Species," Dietz, Barnett, Belote & Aplet (2021) found that 57% of vulnerable U.S. wildlife species have suitable habitat in roadless areas.
Loucks et al. (2003) found that 77% of inventoried roadless areas are critical habitat that have the potential to conserve endangered, threatened or imperiled species.

Roadless areas are critical to maintain such species: "77% of inventoried roadless areas have the potential to conserve threatened, endangered, or imperiled species" (Loucks et al., 2003 https://doi.org/10.5751/ES-00528-070205).

Roadless areas provide needed habitat for 57% of the 537 species of conservation concern that live in the contiguous United States, as documented by this 2021 study by the The Wilderness Society and are a boon to local economies as they offer excellent passive recreational opportunities.

The Forest Service's own researchers found that old-growth stands are critical nesting habitat for northern spotted owls (Lesmeister et al. 2019), and Trout Unlimited's president has pointed out that roadless areas are about 2% of the American landscape but shelter roughly 25% of our threatened and endangered species.

The median roadless area provides habitat for 10 such species, with a maximum of 62 (Dietz et al. 2021). — Matthew S. Dietz, Kevin Barnett, R. Travis Belote, Gregory H. Aplet, 2021 · Global Ecology and Conservation (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gecco.2021.e01943)

wordings: "Section 404 of the Clean Water Act (CWA) establishes a program to regulate the discharge of dredged or fill material into waters of the United States, including wetlands.

Failure to Prevent Severe Degradation of Designated Uses (CWA Section 303) Under Section 303 of the Clean Water Act, states establish water quality standards based on the "designated uses" of a water body—such as drinking water supply, cold-water fisheries, and recreation.

For the Bend Watershed IRA, Deschutes National Forest, the DEIS must disclose the number and location of jurisdictional waters, quantify fill material discharges at each potential stream crossing, and document the Section 404 permitting pathway for each discharge point.

For the Shoal Branch IRA, Chattahoochee National Forest, the DEIS must disclose the number and location of jurisdictional waters, quantify fill material discharges at each potential stream crossing, and document the Section 404 permitting pathway for each discharge point.

For the Tuolumne River IRA, Stanislaus National Forest, the DEIS must disclose the number and location of jurisdictional waters, quantify fill material discharges at each potential stream crossing, and document the Section 404 permitting pathway for each discharge point.

Road construction through the North Fork Middle Fork American River IRA, Tahoe National Forest, necessitates stream crossings where fill material is discharged directly into waters of the United States, each crossing independently requiring Section 404 authorization.

Section 404 requires a permit before dredged or fill material may be discharged into waters of the United States, unless the activity is exempt from Section 404 regulation (e.g., certain farming and forestry activities).

The DEIS must identify every stream crossing in the Big Ridge to South Fork A IRA, White River NF, that would require discharge of fill material into jurisdictional waters and demonstrate how Clean Water Act Section 404 compliance is achieved for each crossing.

A recent analysis from the Center for Biological Diversity estimates that rescission could put more than 400 imperiled species at greater risk, along with millions of acres of designated critical habitat and roughly 1,800 miles of protected rivers and streams.

A recently released report found that rescinding the Roadless Rule would put 7.4 million acres of designated endangered species critical habitat and nearly 1,800 miles of protected rivers and streams at risk — and could hasten the extinction of more than 400 threatened and endangered plants and animals protected under the Endangered Species Act.

According to a new report from the Center for Biological Diversity, rescinding this rule could push more than 400 endangered animal and plant species toward extinction, placing 7.4 million acres of designated endangered species habitat and nearly 1,800 miles of protected rivers and streams in jeopardy.

According to a study referenced by the Center for Biological Diversity, removing the Roadless Rule would put 400 species at risk of extinction, including many animals currently protected under the Endangered Species Act.

Endangered species and habitat loss: A recent study modeling this rescission found it would put roughly 400 species on an "extinction fast track," putting 7.4 million acres of critical habitat and nearly 1,800 miles of protected rivers at risk, threatening 88 species with designated critical habitat in roadless areas.

Far from promoting forest health, this rescission would fragment habitat that is critical to 25% of our endangered animal species and 13% of endangered plant species (according to the Forest Service's own 2001 Record of Decision), jeopardizing the survival of countless species.

More than 400 endangered animal and plant species could face accelerated extinction after the Trump administration’s decision to rescind a rule that has protected old-growth forests for more than two decades.⁠ ⁠ According to a new report from the Center for Biological Diversity, the rollback of the Bill Clinton-era “roadless rule” could put 7.4m acres of endangered-species habitat and nearly 1,800 miles of protected rivers and streams at risk.⁠ ⁠ “Our national forests are home to some of America’s most iconic animals, from grizzlies to hellbenders.

The USDA’s draft environmental impact statement (EIS) also points out that roads are associated with increased human starts, and that new starts are lowest within wilderness areas (p. 86, 90).

The addition of roads of previously roadless areas will also increase the incidence of human-wildlife conflict (p. 151) as well as human-caused fires, with the proportion of human-caused fires in roadless areas often less than half of that in other NDS lands (p. 86, 89; Aplet et al. 2026).
The draft EIS itself says fuels work would reach only a fraction of inventoried roadless acres and that more roads can increase human-caused ignitions.

The notice acknowledges access can increase human-caused ignitions, and the DEIS reports fire scientists warning that more roads could mean more ignitions (p. 101), that ignition rates are currently lower in roadless areas (pp. 24, 89), and that fuel-treatment gains would be modest (p. 225).

The rule itself concedes that greater road access can increase human-caused ignitions, and that only about 24% of these roadless areas overlap the wildland-urban interface where fuel treatment near communities actually matters.

According to the draft environmental impact statement, "As the density of roads increases, so does the probability, number, and frequency of fire ignitions."
Additionally, the DEIS states that “as the density of roads increases, so does the probability, number, and frequency of fire ignitions.”
As the US Forest Service DEIS found, increasing density of roads is correlated with increasing probability, number, and frequency of fire ignitions.

At p. 109 it states that "[r]oad density is linked to human-caused wildfires, and as the density of roads increases so does the probability, number, and frequency of wildfire ignitions (Cardille et al. 2001)."
At page 109, it further acknowledges that increasing road density is associated with increases in the probability, number, and frequency of wildfire ignitions.
But I understand the Draft Environmental Impact Statement itself acknowledges that increased road density raises the likelihood and frequency of human-caused ignitions.
Fire. The DEIS admits that "road density is linked to human-caused wildfires, and as the density of roads increases so does the probability, number, and frequency of wildfire ignitions."

However, the agency's own draft environmental impact statement acknowledges a link between road density and human-caused wildfire ignitions, and independent research has similarly found that wildfires are markedly more likely to start near existing roads than in roadless backcountry.

In the Alternative 2 effects analysis the finding is restated and then set aside: "Road density is linked to human-caused wildfires, and as the density of roads increases so does the probability, number, and frequency of wildfire ignitions (Cardille et al. 2001).

It also states “Road density is linked to human-caused wildfires, and as the density of roads increases so does the probability, number, and frequency of wildfire ignitions” (EIS pp. 87, 90, 101, 105), and the given rebuttal to this statement (about road access) is not logically aligned with the USDA’s claims, as it only serves to lower the implied road density/wildfire correlation risk rather than reverse it.
Second, increased road density is linked to human-caused wildfires with recent research finding that fires are 4 times more likely to start near a road than in a roadless area (Applet et al. 2026).
The DEIS acknowledges that road density is linked to human caused wildfires and that increasing road density increases the probability, number, and frequency of wildfire ignitions.

wordings: A 30-day comment period is too short for an environmental analysis and proposed rule of this magnitude and significance is grossly inadequate and should promptly be extended to a total of at least 120 days.

And unlike 2001, when the original rule was developed over a two-year process that generated more than 1.5 million public comments and 430 public hearings, this rescission is moving forward with no public hearings and just 30 days for public comment- insufficient given the scale of the acreage and resources at stake.
Comment periods should be least 60 days per the Administrative Procedure Act (APA, 5 U.S.C.§553(c)), and Executive Order (EO) 12866, Regulatory Planning and Review.

Given that this rule affects roughly 58.8 million acres across 39 states, why was the public comment period set at 30 days, compared to the 120+ days offered during the 2005 rescission attempt and the extensive public process used to establish the original rule in 2001?

Inadequate public process. The 30-day comment window is unusually short for a proposal of this scale (most DEIS comment periods run 60–90 days), and no public hearings have been held despite hundreds of thousands of Americans — over 99% of prior commenters — opposing this rollback.

Procedural adequacy. Given that this proposal affects nearly 45 million acres across 37 states, and that the original 2001 rule was developed over two years with roughly 600 public hearings, a 30-day comment period with no scheduled public hearings (outside Alaska) does not provide an adequate opportunity for public and technical input commensurate with the scale of this action.
Process concerns. A 45-day comment period is inadequate for a 333-page DEIS affecting 44.7 million acres.

Public input. More than 600,000 comments were submitted during the initial comment period, and the Forest Service itself acknowledges that 99 percent opposed rescission.[7] By comparison, the original rulemaking allowed 129 days for public comment, and the 2005 rescission attempt allowed 182.[7] This proposal initially allowed about a month and was extended only to October 6.[8] A decision affecting roughly 45 million acres warrants far more public engagement.
Such a short comment period for an environmental analysis and proposed rule of this magnitude and significance is grossly inadequate and should promptly be extended.
The Department is now moving forward with a second comment period of only 30 days and, by its own account, no public hearings scheduled in New Hampshire.

The agency allowed the minimum period for public comments (and only that when it became clear it couldn't get away with 30) on the sweeping national rollback affecting roughly 45 million to 58 million acres.
The process is inadequate: A 30-day comment period on a 333-page DEIS covering 44.7 million acres does not permit meaningful public review.
The proposal to undo it allows only about 30 days of comment — far short of what a decision affecting 58.5 million acres and every national forest visitor deserves.
Thirty days is not a meaningful opportunity to comment on a multi-volume Draft EIS, cost-benefit analysis, and Tribal impact statement covering 44.7 million acres.

This comment period is shorter than the 21-day NOI period that 54 members of Congress already called insufficient, despite covering a full proposed rule, draft EIS, and cost-benefit analysis spanning ~45 million acres.
This rescission has been given a fraction of that time for public input, despite affecting the same scale of public land — nearly 45 million acres nationwide.

This rescission proposal initially allowed only a 21-day comment period on the NOI and a 30-day comment period on the DEIS, inadequate to a broad rule that affects nearly 45 million acres all across the nation.

This rescission, affecting 45 million acres, has been advanced with a 21-day comment period and not a single public meeting — despite hundreds of thousands of comments overwhelmingly opposed to weakening these protections.
This rescission, affecting roughly 45 million acres, received a short comment period and no public hearings.

wordings: A rule expected to impose costs an order of magnitude larger than its most optimistic quantified benefits does not meet the standard of reasoned rulemaking required under Executive Order 12866, which the Department itself invokes as governing this action.

An economically significant rule whose own analysis spans from a $92 million loss to a $199 million gain has not shown a benefit; the analysis was published in an agency file folder rather than on the docket, and the rule's claim that impacts "could exceed $100 million" (91 FR 53830) appears with no arithmetic anywhere, though every quantified annual line item is under $22 million.
Every quantified annual line item is under $22 million, yet the rule claims impacts could exceed $100 million, with no arithmetic shown anywhere to support that figure.
Executive Order 12866 requires an accounting of NET benefits, not gross receipts.
I request a single reconciled accounting showing how the claimed benefits outweigh these disclosed costs, particularly given this rule's designation as "economically significant" under E.O. 12866.
It calls the rule economically significant under E.O. 12866 and says impacts "could exceed $100 million," yet certifies no significant impact on small entities under the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

Predictability: “EO. 13563 reaffirms the principles of E.O.12866 while calling for improvements in the Nation’s regulatory system to promote predictability, to reduce uncertainty, and to use the best, most innovative, and least burdensome tools for achieving regulatory ends.“ The best way to promote predictability is not to change the rule!

The Cost Benefit Analysis explains that “the rulemaking would not compel, require, or authorize any site-specific activities” and that “it is difficult to predict quantitative changes in costs or benefits” (p. 20).
The Cost Benefit Analysis itself cannot establish whether this rule gains or loses money.

The Cost Benefit Analysis records at p. 4 that this rule was determined significant for purposes of Executive Order 12866 and requires OMB review, and that Executive Order 13563 “emphasizes the importance of quantifying both costs and benefits, reducing costs, maximizing net benefits.”
The Federal Register states that additional impacts associated with the proposal could exceed $100 million and requests information concerning the range of economic impacts.

The Unfunded Mandates analysis later in the same document states the rule would not compel expenditure of $100 million or more in any one year — a defensible distinction, since that provision measures compelled expenditures rather than aggregate economic effects, but one the document never explains.

wordings: A general goal of "reducing regulatory burden" does not explain why case-by-case forest planning would better protect these areas.

As someone with an academic background in Environmental Studies, I am concerned that shifting decisions over road construction and reconstruction from a consistent national standard to case-by-case local management would expose some of the nation’s remaining intact forest landscapes to avoidable fragmentation, watershed degradation, and long-term public costs.
Finally, replacing one national standard with repeated forest-by-forest planning and project-level disputes may shift rather than eliminate regulatory burden.
Handing that over to be decided forest by forest, plan by plan, means those protections can just disappear depending on who's in charge at the time.
I am also deeply troubled by replacing a national conservation standard with decisions increasingly made forest by forest. Administrations change. Forest plans change.

I am particularly concerned that removing 36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B in its entirety would replace a consistent national conservation standard with a more fragmented approach that could vary significantly among national forests and over time.
I believe those values warrant maintaining a national conservation standard rather than transferring the decision entirely to individual forest-level planning processes.
I do not believe those protection should be eliminated and replaced primarily by a case by case decision at the individual forest level.
It just means fighting the same fight forest by forest, plan by plan, with less public attention every time.
It strips a durable, nationwide standard and leaves roadless areas to be decided forest by forest, plan by plan, and administration by administration.
LOCAL DECISION-MAKING: Forest-by-forest review is not equivalent to a national conservation baseline when the resource (the nation's remaining inventoried roadless lands) is national and finite.
Maintain a consistent national conservation standard rather than relying solely on individual forest-level decisions.

Pushing the decision down to the individual forest planning level, as this proposal does, doesn't add flexibility so much as it removes a durable, nationally consistent baseline and replaces it with a patchwork that will be far easier to erode forest by forest, plan by plan, over time.
Removing 36 CFR Part 294 Subpart B to return decisions entirely to individual forest-level plans undermines a proven national standard.

Replacing a single national standard with case-by-case decisions in hundreds of individual forest plans invites inconsistent, locally pressured outcomes and years of resource-intensive litigation, the opposite of the "efficiency" the agency claims to want.

Replacing this consistent national standard with forest-by-forest, project-level decision-making removes a baseline safeguard and opens these lands to inconsistent management, political pressure, and piecemeal road-building and logging across the country.

The proposal identifies potential local management opportunities, but it does not show that their uncertain benefits outweigh the long-term ecological, recreational, and infrastructure costs of removing a national conservation standard (USDA Forest Service, 2026, pp. 53,828-53,830).

Without it, the only remaining barrier would be case-by-case decisions at the forest and project level, where pressure for new motorized access can be intense and where protections can be revised or weakened over time.

wordings: A 2021 Science of the Total Environment study found unprotected IRAs are important habitat for species of conservation concern, with lasting biodiversity effects if lost (Loucks et al., cited therein).

A peer-reviewed U.S. Forest Service/Wilderness Society analysis found IRAs increase the effective size of, and reduce isolation between, protected areas like national parks and wilderness (Belote et al., 2020).
A third of all IRAs are adjacent to an existing wilderness or national park, and two-thirds are within 1 km of one (Talty et al., 2020).

Because IRAs are in administrative purgatory—not deemed “protected areas,” yet subject to some protections under the Roadless Rule—they may be especially susceptible to the widespread downgrading, downsizing, and degazettement of conservation areas that have occurred recently in the U.S. and throughout the world (Golden Kroner et al., 2019).
Belote et al. (2020) found IRAs capture significant carbon annually relative to already-protected lands.

Formations with the greatest percentage increase in representation when including IRAs in the protected network include Temperate Grassland and Shrubland (57.4%), Cool Temperate Forest and Woodland (52.2%), and Mediterranean Scrub and Grassland (35.5%). — McKinley J. Talty | Kelly Mott Lacroix | Gregory H. Aplet | R. Travis Belote, 2020 · Conservation Science and Practice (https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.288)”
Habitat Fragmentation: IRAs provide continuous wildlife corridors for black bears, deer, and dozens of at-risk species that cannot withstand industrial logging corridors.
IRAs add disproportionately, relative to the area they cover, to the carbon captured by existing protected areas (Talty et al. 2020).
IRAs also buffer and connect existing protected lands, and about one-third of roadless forests border a national park or wilderness area (Talty et al. 2020).
IRAs are essential for the habitat of vulnerable species and acting as a carbon sink (Mildrexler et al., 2026).

If all IRAs were added to the protected-area system in CONUS, there would be a substantial decrease (−38) in the number of wildlife SCCs that are currently considered 'poorly represented' in protected areas. — Global Ecology and Conservation (ScienceDirect), 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gecco.2021.e01943)”

As a resident of California, rescinding the Roadless Rule would destroy something I am proud of in this country: it's natural beauty.

As a resident of NC who has for over a decade delighted in the undisturbed beauty of the Pisgah National Forest and the Blue Ridge region in general, I know that rescinding the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule will harm this precious land.

As a resident of Western North Carolina, an avid hiker, and former volunteer in the Pisgah National Forest Visitor Center, I am daily reminded of the risks and dangers involved in rescinding the Roadless Area Conservation Rule and am vehemently opposed to this unconscionable effort to destroy our natural resources and risk the lives and livelihood of the citizens of our country.

Finally, on a personal note, my best life experiences have been spent hiking in roadless areas in local National Forests, such as the Hardesty Mountain Roadless area, which would lose protection if this rule change occurs.

As a resident of Western North Carolina, an avid hiker, and former volunteer in the Pisgah National Forest Visitor Center, I am daily reminded of the risks and dangers involved in rescinding the Roadless Area Conservation Rule and am vehemently opposed to this unconscionable effort to destroy our natural resources and risk the lives and livelihood of the citizens of our country.

Finally, on a personal note, my best life experiences have been spent hiking in roadless areas in local National Forests, such as the Hardesty Mountain Roadless area, which would lose protection if this rule change occurs.

wordings: "Constructing roads into roadless areas would simply increase the number of fires that need to be suppressed without having a meaningful impact on the likelihood of a large fire igniting." — Aplet, G.H., Hartger, P., Dietz, M.S., 2026 · Fire Ecology (https://doi.org/10.1186/s42408-026-00450-2)
An additional article in the scientific journal Fire Ecology (attached as pdf) shows that building roads in roadless areas is “likely to result in more fires.”
Building permanent road networks into currently unroaded terrain increases the number of ignition sources in the exact landscapes the proposal claims to be protecting.
Creation of roads through these areas create wind tunnels that ramp up fires, while also increasing temperatures 295 feet around the pavement by at least 12 degrees Fahrenheit.
Elsewhere, in a separate three decade study published in Fire Ecology in 2026, results showed that building roads into roadless areas is likely to result in MORE fires.
However, the science shows that roads lead to an increase in fires and that the roadless rule has been effective in reducing fire (Alpet et al. Fire Ecology, 2026).

Increasing roads through our wilderness will not help prevent forest fires, it will simply make this situation all the more common and ruin that peace of the lakes in Jewel Basin and many other places.

Introducing miles of new road infrastructure deeper into our national forests increases, rather than decreases, the long-term wildfire threat to nearby wildland-urban interface (WUI) communities like mine.
Moreover, the University of Washington article notes that research shows roadbuilding in formerly roadless areas can increase fire risk.

The Biological Assessment also warns that its occurrence databases "do not differentiate between DPSes of vertebrate species listed under the ESA, which causes potential inflation of exposure to these entities" (p. 25), so whether the Draft EIS's total counts distinct population segments separately changes the number materially.

The Biological Assessment reports counts only by taxonomic group — for example, "[t]he potential species list from IPaC contained 30 listed or proposed bird species on relevant Forest Service units," of which four were removed and "[t]he 26 potentially present species are organized below" (Draft BA p. 161) — and states no total.

The Biological Assessments record only that species lists "were sent to the Services in September and October 2025 for review" (USFWS BA p. 25) and that "[s]pecies lists and critical habitat were reviewed by the National Marine Fisheries Service in September and October 2025" (NMFS BA p. 22).

The DEIS's invasive-plant section at pp. 114-116 does not mention listed species at all, and the DEIS's ESA discussion refers the reader away, stating that "the Biological Assessments contain the full evaluations for the ESA-listed species and designated critical habitat" (p. 169).

The Draft Biological Assessment discloses its method — IRA shapefiles run through IPaC for the FWS list, NMFS species compiled from consultation records, both lists vetted by Forest Service staff and sent to the Services in September–October 2025, occurrence data from GBIF and NRM (BA p. 25) — but reports counts only by taxonomic group (e.g., 30 candidate bird species, 4 removed, 26 remaining, BA p. 161) and states no total.

The Draft Biological Assessment for USFWS species does disclose a method, and this comment does not suggest otherwise: IRA boundary shapefiles by administrative unit were imported into IPaC to compile the FWS list, NMFS species were compiled from existing consultation documents, both lists were vetted by regional Forest Service staff to remove species that do not occur on National Forest System lands, the lists were sent to the Services for review in September and October 2025, and occurrence data were drawn from GBIF and the Natural Resource Manager (Draft BA, "Species Lists" and "Data Collection and Use," p. 25).

The Final EIS should make a factual correction under 7 CFR 1b.7(f)(2)(v): state the exact number of threatened, endangered, and proposed species in the potentially affected environment, state the date the species lists reflect, state whether distinct population segments are counted separately, and cross-reference the Biological Assessment's Species Lists section at each point the figure is used.

The Forest Service should, in the Final EIS: (1) state the IPaC consultation code and list-generation date underlying the USFWS count, and the date on which the NOAA Fisheries National ESA Critical Habitat Mapper was queried for the NMFS count; (2) state whether the count of 19 includes Southern Oregon/Northern California coho salmon critical habitat, given the Biological Assessment's statement that the designation is absent from the Mapper; (3) reconcile both figures against the critical habitat designations in force at the date of the Final EIS and correct them where designations have been added, revised, or removed since the query; and (4) present in the Biological Assessments the enumeration of critical habitats from which each count is derived, so that the cross-reference at Draft EIS page 168 resolves to the figures it attributes to those documents.
The USFWS Biological Assessment states, at page 25, that "[a] shapefile of IRA boundaries by administrative unit were imported into IPaC to compile the list of species under FWS's jurisdiction."

The agency cannot demonstrate compliance with an executive order it has itself invoked while the record's only quantified statement of invasive-species exposure for listed plants - 81 of 134 taxa, at Biological Assessment p. 344 - is absent from the analysis supporting the decision.
The agency's own Draft Biological Assessment for USFWS species supplies the exposure findings the DEIS would need, and none of them appears in the DEIS.
The statement at page 170 is therefore incomplete as to those species, and it is the agency's own Assessment that establishes it.
This is according to the Pacific Biodiversity Institute’s 2007 study by P. H. Morrison.

An FEIS that carries forward the page 169 exposure screen and the page 168 disclaimer without addressing items 1 through 4 would rest a "likely to adversely affect" finding for 327 species and 71 designated critical habitats on an analysis the agency's own document shows to be incomplete, and would be arbitrary and capricious under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A).

By the agency's own account the source of the count of 19 omits at least one designation, and neither the Draft EIS nor the Biological Assessment says whether the 19 includes the SONCC coho designation.
In addition, the USFWS Biological Assessment concedes the limits of its own inputs.

wordings: I ask the agency to reconcile this contradiction in its supporting record and explain, specifically, how the rule caused the forest health harm it describes when its own findings point the other way.

I request a factual correction to the Rationale for the Proposed Rule under 7 CFR 1b.7(f)(2)(v), reconciling it with Table 14, Table 21, and the activity figures at pp. 14–15 — either by withdrawing the forest-health causal chain, or by stating, region by region and against those tables, where roadless designation is in fact associated with worse forest-health outcomes than active management.

I want the agency to explain, specifically and on the record, how it squares the forest health justification with its own data showing the rule's constraints on fuel treatment were minimal and that roadless areas often carry lower insect risk than managed land.

That claim is not reconciled with what the document itself reports elsewhere: that the rule did not meaningfully constrain fuel treatments as a share of forested land, and that insect and disease risk in western roadless areas is similar to or lower than on managed forest land outside those designations.

The agency cannot in good faith blame the rule for forest health failures while its own findings show the rule was not a meaningful barrier to treatment and that roadless areas often carry lower pest risk than managed land.

The agency must reconcile its forest health justification with its own data showing the rule was not a meaningful constraint on fuel treatment and that insect risk is often lower inside roadless areas.

The agency must reconcile its forest health rationale with its own cited research showing the rule's minimal effect on fuel treatment capacity and its own data on insect risk before issuing any final rule.

The agency must reconcile its forest health rationale with its own findings that the rule's constraint on fuel treatments was marginal and that insect risk is often lower in roadless areas, and must explain why road construction follows from either of those findings.

The agency must reconcile that contradiction before it proceeds, explaining on the record how a rule that the document says did not significantly limit fuel treatments still produced the forest health emergency the rationale describes.

The agency must reconcile the forest health justification with its own findings that the rule's practical constraint on fuel treatment was limited and that roadless western forests often carry no greater disease burden than managed ones.

The agency must reconcile this forest health rationale with its own findings that the rule did not meaningfully constrain fuel treatments and that insect risk is often lower in roadless areas, and it must do so in a responsive, substantive way before finalizing this rule.
The agency needs to reconcile the forest health rationale with its own findings before this rule can move forward.
The forest health rationale in the proposal is in tension with the agency's own findings.
The forest health rationale offered for rescission is also in tension with the agency's own findings.

The forest health rationale rests on a conclusion the agency's own data undercuts, and I want the agency to reconcile that contradiction squarely, explaining how the rule harmed forest health when its own findings suggest insect risk is often lower where the rule applies.
The solitude I seek and the birds I hope to see depend on forests that the agency's own data suggest are not in the crisis condition the rationale implies.

wordings: A great example of the consequences of building roads and logging in roadless areas in upper watersheds in Salem, Oregon in 1996, when the city had to spend $100 million on new water treatment infrastructure after mass sedimentation from those human activities was washed into the watershed by large storms.

wordings: As a regular visitor to the White Mountain National Forest, the justification provided by USDA Deputy Secretary Stephen Alexander Vaden, claiming that a nationwide rollback is required to grant "access" for active forest management and wildfire reduction, is explicitly contradicted by the agency’s own data.
BiOps are not currently required to formally quantify no-action fire risk to listed species.
Broad rescission is not required to address wildfire risk, and could increase ignition sources in areas that are currently among the least fire-prone due to their undeveloped condition.
Flawed Fire-Management Justification: The Forest Service's claim that repealing the rule is necessary for wildfire management contradicts its own historical data.
Flawed Wildfire Justifications: The Forest Service claims that rescinding the rule is necessary for wildfire mitigation, yet the agency's own data contradicts this.
How does the USDA reconcile the existing research with the justification of rescission with regard to wildfire risk?
If no such data exists, on what basis is wildfire risk reduction being used to justify this rule?

Specifically, on page 26 the regulatory impact analysis document states that “wildfire risk reduction in IRAs is not quantified in this analysis,” yet the document assumes that there would be some reduction of risk.
The Department's central justification, that rescission is needed to reduce wildfire risk, does not hold up, and the Forest Service's own analysis undermines it.

The Forest Service's primary justification—that eliminating the rule is necessary to grant local managers the "flexibility" to mitigate wildfire risks—is directly contradicted by the agency’s own data.
The administration’s claim that repealing the rule is necessary for wildfire mitigation is contradicted by agency data and independent science.
The agency’s own analysis indicates that rescinding the rule is unlikely to produce meaningful reductions in overall wildfire risk. (Pew Charitable Trusts⁠)
The proposal asserts that rescinding the rule will improve wildfire management.
The proposal does not demonstrate that nationwide rescission would materially reduce wildfire risk (USDA Forest Service, 2026, pp. 53,828-53,829).

Wildfire Risk and Management Contradictions: The agency’s rationale that repealing the rule is necessary for wildfire management directly contradicts established science and the Forest Service’s own data.
Wildfire: The proposed rule presents rescission as a wildfire prevention tool, but the agency's own analysis of human caused ignitions during 2014-2024 undercuts the stated benefits.

wordings: A National Parks and Conservation Association analysis found that of the approximately 45 million acres of designated roadless areas in national forests, nearly 30% (17.5 million acres) are within 30 miles of national park lands.

Access to Outdoor Recreation: A study by National Parks Conservation Association (NPCA) found that nearly 30% (17.5 million acres) of the 45 million acres of designated roadless areas in national forests are within 30 miles of national park lands.
According to the spatial data regarding the GWNF North River District, this constitutes the largest concentration of roadless acreage in the eastern United States.

An AllTrails analysis found 15 of the 50 most popular hikes nationwide within inventoried roadless areas are in the White Mountain National Forest alone, a forest with well under 1% of total National Forest System acreage.
An NPCA analysis found that out of 45 millions acres of roadless areas in national forests, about 17.5 million are within 30 miles of national park lands.
Fourth, NPCA analysis found nearly 30% (17.5 million acres) of the public lands protected by the roadless rule are within 30 miles of national park lands.

Inventoried roadless areas make up just 2% of the lower 48 states; in New England, the White and Green Mountain National Forests together hold roughly 260,000 roadless acres, and reporting indicates the White Mountains alone could lose up to 235,000 protected acres under this proposal [6,7].
Irreplaceable Old-Growth Protection: According to the U.S. Forest Service’s own inventory data, one-third of all National Forest old-growth areas are located within protected Roadless Areas.
Roadless areas compromise about 30% of all national forest land and protect many of our last wild places, imperiled species and old growth forests.

The 58.5 million acres inventoried as roadless are spread throughout 120 national forests located in 38 States and the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico (https://www.fs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/roadless/roadless-feis-summary.pdf), A total of 50.3 million acres of protected wilderness areas, roadless areas, and designated critical habitat, as well as 2,300 miles of wild and scenic rivers are included in the emergency declaration map area, fast-tracking destructive projects in areas that were intentionally set aside to preserve their natural values and functions (Woodard et al., 2025).

The Bridger unit at 45,059 acres, the Hyalite-Porcupine-Buffalo Horn Wilderness Study Area at 143,991 acres, the Madison at 127,859 acres, and the North Absaroka at 159,075 acres form part of the northeastern wall of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem.
The Economic Analysis supplies the exposure distribution at p. 18: 51.5 percent of affected roadless acreage lies within one mile of a road, and 30.8 percent within a half mile.
The Forest Service’s broader data identify approximately 1.47 million acres of inventoried roadless areas in the New England/Acadia ecoregion.

The Gallatin's roadless inventory alone encompasses 14 areas totaling 703,144 acres, forming part of the northeastern wall of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem alongside the Crazy Mountains and the Absaroka-Beartooth.
The roadless rule covers about 30% of National Forest land and protects habitat for about 1600 species. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roadless_area_conservation
Trout Unlimited's read of Forest Service data puts 32 percent of Wyoming's treated National Forest acreage inside inventoried roadless areas, done under exceptions the current rule already contains.

wordings: A 2024 study in Forests found that forest roads can contribute up to 90% of the sediment loads in streams.

According to the Journal of Soil and Water Conservation, “Logging roads have been linked to great increases in erosion rates and sediment delivery to streams – up to 850% over rates in undisturbed habitat” (Della Sala, D.A., Karr, J.R., Olson, DM.,2011 • Journal of Soil and Water Conservation).
Areas with logging roads, as contemplated by this rule change, have up to 850% more erosion than undisturbed habitat.

Because inventoried roadless areas contain few or no roads today, rescission would introduce precisely the sediment source the agency's own research identifies as the leading driver of stream sedimentation — directly threatening the cold-water trout streams of roadless areas like South Mills River in the Pisgah National Forest.

Forest Service Southern Research Station studies of national forest roads in the Southeast measured average soil losses of 276 tons per hectare from road sections, with eroded sediment traveling a mean of 30 meters downslope into the forest floor (Grace 2005; Grace and Elliot 2008).

But the 2020 figures for suitable old growth acreage depend on a Tongass plan timber suitability change that the document indicates was never issued.

I request a factual correction under 7 CFR 1b.7(f)(2)(v): that the Final EIS identify the source and effective date of both figures, and conform them to a current, identified national wilderness inventory as of the date of the Final EIS, giving the current figures wherever they differ from 111.9 million and 36.7 million acres.

I request a factual correction under 7 CFR 1b.7(f)(2)(v): that the Final EIS name the source of the 36.7-million-acre National Forest System wilderness figure and the date as of which that source was current, and state, where the effects analysis relies on the figure, how it supports the finding that designated wilderness provides recreation opportunity comparable to inventoried roadless areas.

I request that the Final EIS do one of two things: (1) identify the source of both the 111.9-million-acre National Wilderness Preservation System total and the 36.7-million-acre National Forest System subset, state the date to which each is current, and add that source to the literature cited; or (2) if no source supports the figures as stated, correct them.

If the Tongass figure has moved since the inventory from which it was taken — as the Draft EIS's own account of Chief-approved technical corrections indicates it may have — then the acreage the Draft EIS reports as removed from roadless protection under alternatives 2 and 3, the residual it reports as retained under alternative 3, and the baseline against which every alternative's effects are measured are each misstated by the same amount.

It then carries the Tongass figure without stating when the Tongass inventory was last corrected, what any such correction changed, or the date as of which the "current national roadless area maps" it relies on at page 21 are current.

I request a factual correction under 7 CFR 1b.7(f)(2)(v): that the Final EIS name the source of the 36.7-million-acre National Forest System wilderness figure and the date as of which that source was current, and state, where the effects analysis relies on the figure, how it supports the finding that designated wilderness provides recreation opportunity comparable to inventoried roadless areas.

I request that the Final EIS do one of two things: (1) identify the source of both the 111.9-million-acre National Wilderness Preservation System total and the 36.7-million-acre National Forest System subset, state the date to which each is current, and add that source to the literature cited; or (2) if no source supports the figures as stated, correct them.

state whether the alternative 2 / alternative 3 acreage differential at p. 115 survives the acknowledged undercount, or withdraw that differential as a basis for distinguishing the alternatives.

wordings: A 2026 study in Biological Conservation found that Inventoried Roadless Areas are among the highest-integrity forests in the country and provide important benefits including healthy watersheds, biodiversity, and climate regulation.
According to Mildrexler et. al, 2026, protected forests, including IRAs, score a higher integrity index than forests that are not protected (Mildrexler et al., 2026; see attached paper and figure).
An analysis in Conservation Science and Practice (Talty et al., 2020) found that roadless areas also add substantially to carbon storage on protected lands.

David J. Mildrexler, Logan T. Berner, Beverly E. Law, Mary S. Booth, Roadless rule rescission threatens highest integrity forest ecosystems in the United States, Biological Conservation, Volume 321, 2026, 111950, ISSN 0006-3207, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2026.111950.

In the Roadless Rule FEIS Summary (November 2000, page S-1), the Introduction states that inventoried roadless “areas possess social and ecological values and characteristics that are becoming scarce in an increasingly developed landscape” and that “these areas provide a bulwark against the spread of nonnative invasive plant species”.
Logging within IRAs runs counter to the urgent need to prevent forest degradation of intact forest ecosystems (Moomaw et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2024; Watson et al., 2016).

Old growth forests are incredibly important for the environment – they sequester large amounts of carbon from the air to produce oxygen, provide unique microclimates that support endangered species such as the Northern Spotted Owl and the Del Norte salamander, and create ideal soil conditions for the next generation of trees to thrive (Gilhen-Baker, et al.) Allowing timber harvesting within inventoried roadless areas would put these old-growth forests at risk and would likely result in a major loss of biodiversity, especially in the Western U.S. where these forests are concentrated.
Old-growth forests can be considered a a non-renewable resource; in Southeast Alaska, a clearcut stand needs two to three centuries to redevelop old-growth structure.

Recent research further demonstrates that Inventoried Roadless Areas contain some of the nation's highest-integrity forests and provide significant benefits including clean water, biodiversity, carbon storage, wildlife habitat, climate regulation, and cultural values (Mildrexler et al., Berner, Law & Booth, 2026).

Roadless rule rescission threatens highest integrity forest ecosystems in the United States, Biological Conservation, Volume 321, 2026, 111950, ISSN 0006-3207, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2026.111950.
Separately, and as a distinct request: the Draft EIS's reference list includes Frey et al. 2016, "Spatial models reveal the microclimatic buffering capacity of old-growth forests," Science Advances.

Separately, research on intact forest systems indicates that ecological integrity buffers against the disturbances rescission proponents cite (think insect outbreaks, disease, drought) rather than amplifying them (Rogers et al., 2022, Frontiers in Forests and Global Change).
The Forest Service’s analysis utilizing the Forest Landscape Integrity Index reveals that Inventoried Roadless Areas maintain the highest integrity scores in the nation (a median score of 9.5).

The regenerative forestry practices the Forest Service and the Missouri Department of Conservation have expanded in the Mark Twain are improving habitat and increasing biodiversity, and those gains rest partly on the landscape integrity this rule maintains.

wordings: As a person who grew up in rural Oregon during the 1990’s environmental rulings, I watched our local economies crash, schools suffer, and a long-term decline in recreational opportunities across the forest landscape.

For us rural Oregonians, rescinding the roadless rule isn't just threatening where we like to play on the weekends: rescinding the roadless rules will threaten our homes due to fire risk, our livelihoods, since our area is almost 100% dependent on recreation economy, and our quality of life here, which is inextricably linked to the presence of undisturbed habitat for the animals we hunt, the plants we forage, and the water we drink.
Instead, increasing roads will damage recreation areas, scenic views, and wildlife habitat, and eliminate the core reasons people choose to live, work, and play in Central Oregon.
Logging these areas would bring little return to Central Oregon while damaging the scenery, recreation, and habitat that draw people to live and visit here.

Opening roadless areas to logging in central Oregon will not yield a meaningful economic return, but rather it will damage recreation areas, scenic views, and wildlife habitat, and eliminate the core reasons people choose to live, work, and recreate within Central Oregon.
Over thirty-five years living in rural Southern Oregon, including thirty years in the Applegate Valley, I have watched a marked decrease in wildlife, in particular insects and other pollinators.
Putting its 235,000 acres of roadless wilderness at risk through rescission of the Roadless Rule negatively impacts those opportunities and the local economies that depend on them.
Rather, roads will damage important recreation areas, scenic views, and fish & wildlife habitat, and would wreck the core reasons people choose to live, work, and recreate in Central Oregon.
Repealing the Roadless Act will devastate local economies including where I’ve spent much of my life, and currently vote, the northwest counties of North Carolina.
Rescinding the Roadless Rule could have a negative affect on the economy of Mount Shasta City, California near where I live.

The repeal of the roadless rule in the Tongass negatively impacts local economies in Southeast Alaska.
There is nothing good to be gained from it and instead it would bring forever harm to Oregon forests.

I request that the FEIS supplement the Tribal Rights and Interests analysis to do what the DEIS presently does not: for each tribe whose treaty-reserved rights the record identifies — including at minimum the Swinomish Indian Tribal Community, the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes of the Flathead Nation, and the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes — (1) identify the treaty and the rights reserved; (2) map the inventoried roadless acreage lying within the ceded territory, usual-and-accustomed area, or identified subsistence use area to which those rights attach; (3) state, by alternative, the acres of that overlap in which road construction and timber harvest would become permissible; and (4) analyze the effect of that change on the quantity, quality, and ecological integrity of the treaty resources on which, by the DEIS's own statement at p. 210, the usability of the right depends.

Page 146 of the draft Environmental Impact Statement specifically discusses potential negative effects on biodiversity due to timber harvesting, mentioning “declines in abundance for some species”, using the loss of habitat for martens tied to timber harvesting the late 1980s as an example.
