At pp. 165–166 the Draft EIS concludes that road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvest "could potentially have long-term adverse effects on biodiversity by increasing habitat fragmentation, loss of connectivity, negative edge effects, and human disturbance"; that "[t]hese impacts would likely be more frequent and broader in scale under alternative 2"; that impacts under alternative 3 "would likely have a lesser effect on biodiversity than alternative 2"; and that impacts "would likely be the least under alternative 1."

Page 146 of the draft Environmental Impact Statement specifically discusses potential negative effects on biodiversity due to timber harvesting, mentioning “declines in abundance for some species”, using the loss of habitat for martens tied to timber harvesting the late 1980s as an example.

Pursuant to the DEIS (Vol. 1, Pg 29): “In general, impacts from road construction and timber harvest activities could include: increased fire frequency (human-caused), reduction in primitive or semi-primitive recreational settings; sedimentation and impacts to water quality; landscape fragmentation; adverse impacts to threatened, endangered, or sensitive wildlife and plants; loss of scenic character; impacts to tribally important resources; or economic losses related to recreation or non-commodity values of Roadless areas.”
Road construction and logging “could potentially have long-term negative impacts” on historic and archaeological sites nationwide (p. 196)
The DEIS acknowledges that road construction and timber harvest activities could have “adverse impacts to threatened, endangered, or sensitive wildlife and plants.”

The agency's analysis specifically recognizes road construction and timber harvest as major risks for altering and fragmenting roadless landscapes.

wordings: As cited in the US Small Business Administration (USBA) the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) states that if an estimated 4.8 million acres of forest out of the Roadless Rules ~58.5 million acres of protected forest was logged this could increase the United States timber harvest by 5-10%, and result in $4.6-10.6 million dollars in revenue per year for the timber industry.

However, the summary of potential impacts states rescinding the 2001 Roadless rule “could” increase the annual saw timber harvest by only 5-10% ($5-11million in Forest Service and Treasury Revenues), and this increase is described as “unlikely.”

Meanwhile, the benefits the agency quantifies for rescission are commercial: about 4.8 million acres newly available for timber harvest and a 5 to 10 percent increase in national forest sawtimber harvest, along with expanded access for mineral and energy development.

Should the roadless rule be rescinded to assist with building the timber industry, it is forecasted that there would only be a 5-10% increase in revenue should all impacted land be used for this purpose.

Specifically, the U.S. Small Business Administration estimates that the increase in the timber harvest that would result from the abandonment of the Roadless Rule would generate $4.6-10.6 M a year in increased timber industry revenue.
The DEIS explicitly notes that the potential benefits of this rescission to the timber industry are not expected to be substantial.

The Forest Service estimates rescission could open roughly 4.8 million acres to logging, raise harvest volume 5 to 10 percent, and generate an additional $4.6 to $10.6 million per year for the timber industry.

The Forest Service's own analysis acknowledges that rescinding the rule would expand opportunities for timber harvesting and could provide millions of dollars in additional annual revenue to the timber industry.

The PRIA estimates that rescission could increase timber harvests by roughly 5–10% nationally, generating $5–$11 million annually for the Treasury and Forest Service, and a similar amount for industry.

The proposed rule frames this action primarily as reducing "regulatory burden," but the rule's own impact analysis shows the practical benefits are modest: an estimated 5–10% increase in annual timber harvest generating $5.2–11.4 million per year, weighed against removing 25 years of protection from 58.5 million acres of currently roadless national forest.
The proposed rule itself acknowledges considerable uncertainty about how much additional timber production would actually result from rescission.
The proposed rule itself acknowledges economic benefits from increased timber harvest and greater flexibility for resource development.

USDA's own analysis projects the rescission would raise national timber harvest volume by only 5-10%, generating an estimated $4.6-$10.6 million per year in additional industry revenue — a small benefit to justify eliminating protections across tens of millions of acres.

wordings: According to the Draft Environmental Impact Statement (DEIS) repealing the roadless rule would “adversely affect” threatened and endangered species including Bull trout.
According to the Forest Service’s data in the DEIS, 327 threatened and endangered species would be directly impacted by reversal of the Roadless Rule.
Also, the Forest Service’s biological assessment found that removing the Roadless Rule is “likely to adversely affect” 327 threatened and endangered species and 71 designated critical habitats.

BACKGROUND. The proposal would remove 36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B, ending national limits on roads and timber harvest.

I am commenting on the proposed rescission of 36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B, which restricts road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvest in inventoried roadless areas, and on the accompanying Draft Environmental Impact Statement (DEIS).

I support the repeal 36 CFR 294 subpart B, which established prohibitions on road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas on National Forest System lands.
Rescinding 36 CFR 294 subpart B removes the prohibition on road construction for all purposes, not just fuels treatment.
Rescinding 36 CFR part 294, subpart B would lift the national limits on road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting across inventoried roadless areas.
The proposal would remove and reserve 36 CFR part 294, subpart B, ending the 2001 prohibitions on road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvest in inventoried roadless areas.
The proposal would remove protections in 36 C.F.R. part 294, subpart B, which restrict most new road construction, road reconstruction, and commercial timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas.
The proposed removal and reservation of 36 CFR part 294, subpart B would eliminate the national protections established by the Roadless Rule.

The proposed rule would remove and reserve 36 CFR part 294, subpart B, thereby eliminating the national-level restrictions on road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas.

The proposed rule would remove the nationwide protections against road construction, road reconstruction and timber harvesting that have applied to inventoried roadless areas since 2001\. According to the proposal, USDA seeks to remove the national protections that limit road construction, road reconstruction, and certain timber-harvesting activities in inventoried roadless areas, returning these decisions to individual forest planning processes.
BACKGROUND. The proposal would remove 36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B, ending national limits on roads and timber harvest.

I am commenting on the proposed rescission of 36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B, which restricts road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvest in inventoried roadless areas, and on the accompanying Draft Environmental Impact Statement (DEIS).

I support the repeal 36 CFR 294 subpart B, which established prohibitions on road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas on National Forest System lands.
Rescinding 36 CFR 294 subpart B removes the prohibition on road construction for all purposes, not just fuels treatment.
Rescinding 36 CFR part 294, subpart B would lift the national limits on road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting across inventoried roadless areas.
The proposal would remove and reserve 36 CFR part 294, subpart B, ending the 2001 prohibitions on road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvest in inventoried roadless areas.
The proposal would remove protections in 36 C.F.R. part 294, subpart B, which restrict most new road construction, road reconstruction, and commercial timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas.
The proposed removal and reservation of 36 CFR part 294, subpart B would eliminate the national protections established by the Roadless Rule.

The proposed rule would remove and reserve 36 CFR part 294, subpart B, thereby eliminating the national-level restrictions on road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas.

The proposed rule would remove the nationwide protections against road construction, road reconstruction and timber harvesting that have applied to inventoried roadless areas since 2001\. ([Federal Register](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/20/2026-16965/special-areas-roadless-area-conservation?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

The rule under review, published in the Federal Register on August 20, 2026 (91 FR 53827), would remove and reserve 36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B in its entirety, eliminating the national prohibition on new road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting across 58.5 million acres of inventoried roadless areas nationwide.
stands_for: According to the proposal, USDA seeks to remove the national protections that limit road construction, road reconstruction, and certain timber-harvesting activities in inventoried roadless areas, returning these decisions to individual forest planning processes.

wordings: A 2020 study by Taxpayers for Commonsense found that in Alaska’s Tongass National Forest alone, over the previous four decades, the Forest Service spent nearly $2 billion preparing and administering timber sales, while bringing in just $227 million in revenue, resulting in a net loss of about $1.73 billion.

According to Taxpayers for Common Sense’s analysis Cutting Our Losses: Twenty Years of Money-Losing Timber Sales in the Tongass, the past two decades of timber sales and returns in the Tongass have lost federal taxpayers $600 million.

According to the Forest Service's own analysis, from 2005 through 2014 the agency spent an average of approximately $12.5 million per year administering Tongass timber sales while receiving only about $1.1 million per year in timber-sale revenue—a net difference of roughly $11.4 million annually, before accounting for road construction costs.

For example, given that the cost of building and maintaining roads is estimated to cost as much as $6.9 Billion, and the estimated 5 to 10 percent increase in annual timber harvest is not mandated, unlikely due to budgets, unforeseen limits on operability, and market conditions, and estimated to yield revenue in the 10s of millions, repealing the 2021 Roadless Rule seems likely increase costs without material benefit.

Studies reported by that group and by Taxpayers for Common Sense indicate the Forest Service often spends more to prepare and administer timber sales than it earns from them.[9] Building roads into remote, marginal areas would add costs the agency is already unable to meet.

Taxpayers have subsidized the Tongass timber program at a rate of over $25 million per year, with individual timber sales like Big Thorne losing roughly ten dollars for every dollar of revenue generated.

wordings: As documented in the Alternatives Considered but Eliminated from Detailed Study section, "An alternative that considered maintaining existing inventoried roadless area boundaries and prohibitions on permanent road construction while allowing temporary road construction and timber harvest was considered but eliminated from detailed study as not being responsive to the purpose and need."

Most importantly, the DEIS states that the Forest Service considered but eliminated an alternative that would retain existing roadless boundaries and the prohibition on permanent road construction while allowing temporary roads and timber harvest.
The Alternatives Considered but Eliminated section documents this elimination.

The DEIS states that Alternatives with more protection were dismissed as not responsive to the deregulatory executive orders, and the keep-boundaries option was cut because it "would continue to restrict local decision-making discretion" and because analysing roadless values is "an administrative and legal burden for the agency."

wordings: As the spouse of a federal wildland firefighter and a resident of the Salt Lake Valley, I have three primary concerns with rescission: wildfire and firefighter safety; impacts to water and air quality; and the loss of roadless characteristics that directly affects my family and our public lands.
I ask USDA to carefully consider the effects that rescinding these protections could have on forests, wildlife, water resources, outdoor recreation, and families who value these public lands.

In closing, for the reasons I have discussed, fully or partially rescinding the Roadless Area Conservation Rule would not benefit humans by reducing wildfires and would negatively affect plants and animals important to Western North Carolina.

In my home tate, rescinding the Roadless Rule would negatively impact our watershed, increase the likelihood of wildfires (see: https://westernpriorities.org/2026/08/the-forest-services-own-review-finds-repealing-the-roadless-rule-could-increase-wildfire-risk-and-harm-communities/), and indubitably threaten endangered species.

My concerns with rescinding the roadless rule include, but are not limited to: 1) An increase in human-caused wildfires, 2) destruction of habitat for sensitive plants and animals, 3) DECREASED recreational opportunities for locals and tourists in Oregon, 4) lack of resources to support the current roads and infrastructure.
Rescinding their protections would increase—not reduce—the risks facing Oregon’s communities, watersheds, and wildlife.
Rescission will threaten vital backcountry ecosystems, clean drinking water sources, and wildlife habitats (for salmon, elk, grizzly bears and others), as well as thousands of miles of public trails.

The DEIS clearly shows that this reckless action would devastate our public lands, waste taxpayer resources, and undermine the clean water, wildlife habitat, and recreation opportunities that millions of Americans depend on for their livelihoods and well-being.
The Forest Service should identify Oregon roadless areas vulnerable to new roads or commercial timber activity and the resulting cumulative effects.
The agency should say plainly, on the record, what share of remaining old growth in Oregon would be exposed to road construction and timber extraction if those areas lose their protection.

The roadless rule's recission will increase wildfire risk, endanger the water quality of people living in WNC who are still struggling to recover from Hurricane Helene, damage what little remaining contiguous green space remains in the US (Heilman, Strittholt, Slosser & DellaSala 2002; Dinerstein, Buotte, Law et al. 2021), destroy ecotourism industries in WNC with financial losses that cannot be fully recovered from timber sales, threaten the survival of many endemic endangered and threatened species (Loucks et al. 2003; Trombulak & Frissell 2000), and remove critical carbon sequestering vegetation from our state (DellaSala, Mackey, Norman, Campbell, Comer, Kormos, Keith & Rogers, 2022).

As someone who frequently uses and values the Tongass National Forest for recreation, I am deeply concerned about the negative impacts that removing these protections will have on this irreplaceable ecosystem.

As someone who values public lands for recreation, clean water, environmental Stability and future generations, I am deeply concerned that removing protections from 45 million acres of national forests will fragment critical wildlife habitats, degrade vital watersheds, and increase erosion.
Few states are under more development pressure than Florida, which is already pushing wildlife into small, isolated pockets of quality habitat.

Florida has many issues with development and harmful environmental policies, which is why I've become deeply involved in the policies and actions our government takes, doing what I can to be proactive and raise awareness in my community.
Florida’s continuing loss and fragmentation of wildlife habitat make remaining intact public lands increasingly important.

I care deeply about the future of our public lands, and I am asking the U.S. Forest Service to act as a responsible steward of these forests rather than opening them up to commercial logging, mining, and road construction.
I've personally seen hundreds if not thousands of acres of wetlands absolutely destroyed by subdivision development in my state of Illinois.
Managing these public lands responsibly requires protecting them from extractive activities that would compromise the fragile ecosystems within them.

It also implements Executive Order 14153, Unleashing Alaska's Extraordinary Resource Potential, which specifically directs the Forest Service to exempt the Tongass from the Roadless Rule.
Returning these decisions solely to local officials, while explicitly excluding the Tongass under Executive Order 14153, prioritizes short-term resource extraction over the long-term public interest.
This exclusion is driven by Executive Order 14153, not by scientific assessment or land management planning.

wordings: A 2019 study, [Decline of the North American avifauna, in the journal Science, (19 Sep 2019, Vol 366, Issue 6461, pp. 120-124) ] reported that bird populations had plummeted by 70% in the last 50 years.

Building new roads into Northern Massanutten and the other roadless areas across Virginia's 393,682 acres spread across 64 inventoried roadless areas would do exactly that: it would destroy the forested habitat that our native bird species like the cardinal depend on, and it would replace the quiet that makes birdwatching possible with the kind of noise the agency's own cited research shows drives birds away.

Forest interior migratory bird species tend to be vulnerable to predation and parasitism because they often have open cup nest structures, poorly developed defense mechanisms, nest close to the ground and typically only produce a single, relatively small clutch each breeding season. — USDA Forest Service, Gallatin National Forest Travel Plan FEIS - Issue 14: Migratory Birds, 2006 (https://www.fs.usda.gov/media/53140)”

Habitat loss and the resulting fragmentation on the breeding grounds are strongly correlated with observed population declines for the Connecticut warbler, which has experienced a total population decline of 62% since 1966 and declined by −8.99% per year between 2000 and 2017.

I am also a bird-watcher and know that we have lost 2.9 billion birds since 1970, primarily because of loss of native plants and habitat and the rise of development (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 2025).

NABCI also reports that “…over 50% of western forest birds are declining due to habitat degradation from fire suppression and industrial timber management…” which has disrupted the mosaic of large old-growth areas and conifer and broadleaf forests that existed in the past.

The US Fish and Wildlife Service says the Wood Thrush “is likely to experience range contractions as a result of habitat loss and climate change” and lists the bird as “one of its highest conservation priorities” (https://www.fws.gov/species/wood-thrush-hylocichla-mustelina).
The agency's DEIS also notes that upland birds need complex forest structure and that some show site fidelity that limits how far they can adapt when habitat changes.
The birds and wildlife I go to observe in the White Mountains depend on interior forest conditions that roads directly degrade.

The scrub-jay population has declined 90% in the past century largely due to habitat destruction, fragmentation and degradation from development. (https://myfwc.com/wildlifehabitats/profiles/birds/songbirds/florida-scrub-jay/)

wordings: Dismantling national protections across roughly 45 million acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) threatens intact wildlife habitat, clean drinking water sources, and local outdoor recreation economies—all while ignoring the agency’s own historical mandate to preserve these unroaded lands.

I urge the Forest Service to select Alternative 1 (the No Action Alternative) and maintain the full protections currently in place for our nation’s 58 million acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs).As someone who deeply values our public lands for backcountry recreation, fish and wildlife habitat, and clean water, I am incredibly concerned about the long-term impacts of opening these pristine areas to road construction and commercial timber harvesting.

Permitting commercial road construction and industrial timber harvesting in Washington’s 2 million acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) will permanently degrade the scenic backdrops and wilderness experiences that draw tourists to our shops, hotels, and guide services.

Removing national prohibitions on road construction and commercial timber harvesting across nearly 45 million acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) will cause irreversible damage to our public lands, water supplies, and local economies.

Rescinding blanket protections across 58.5 million acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) threatens headwater drinking supplies, critical fish and wildlife habitat, and vital backcountry recreation, while failing to meet basic legal requirements.

Rescinding protections across approximately 45 million acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas compromises critical wildlife habitat, municipal drinking watersheds, carbon storage, and the foundational grounds of our national outdoor heritage.
Rescinding these federal protections places 172,000 acres of IRA at immediate risk of commercial logging, industrial development, habitat-fragmentation and motorized uses on non-motorized trails.

Rescinding this rule and removing protections for 58.5 million acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas across 39 states could endanger water supplies, destroy habitats for endangered species, and scar the old-growth forests I have come to know in my time as a land surveyor.

Stripping these protections threatens to open roughly 50,000 acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) across Florida’s three national forests—Apalachicola, Osceola, and Ocala—to destructive road construction and commercial timber harvesting.

The proposed rule change to open 44 million acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) to road building and commercial logging is scientifically unsound, counterproductive to wildfire mitigation, and damaging to fish and wildlife habitat.
